content.title: Review
content.review:
This paper presents NASLib, a code repository for performing NAS experiments. The motivation for doing this is sound, as reproducibility is a key problem in NAS (https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.12522v3). However, actual implementation seems limited.

I don’t think a code repo should be published as a research paper at a top machine learning conference unless it is a game-changer. A good example of this is BackPACK (https://openreview.net/pdf?id=BJlrF24twB) from ICLR 2020. Its primary contribution is a codebase that facilitated computations that were previously too expensive in PyTorch e.g. getting individual sample weight gradients on the backward pass.  It opened the door to a whole suite of feasible new optimisers in Python. 

By contrast, it doesn’t appear to me that this codebase allows NAS researchers to do anything new. It provides a wrapper for running NAS experiments that there is already good open-source code for (e.g. https://github.com/D-X-Y/AutoDL-Projects). The authors use the original DARTS code as an example of what needs remedying but this is 2 years old and has been improved in other repos.
 
It is quite sparse in terms of the actual spaces and optimisers defined. There is an emphasis on one-shot methods and no code for REINFORCE. As this is so prevalent in the NAS literature (https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.01578, https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.07012,https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.03268) then this is a fairly glaring omission. The list of improvements planned in the paper emphasises that this is not finished work.

The authors point out that there are other libraries for this purpose (https://github.com/microsoft/archai, https://github.com/walkerning/aw_nas) that “aren’t yet published” and these are not mentioned again. Firstly, I don’t think it is particularly important that there exists a published conference paper to supplement a code repo. Secondly, a comparison is needed. Why should I use this library over those libraries? What are the functional differences, limitations etc.

The evaluation consists of results comparisons to existing code. The DARTS performance in Table 1 is very different. Is there an obvious reason for this?

There are no research contributions, the technical contributions seem limited. I don’t see what this library provides that doesn’t already exist in the ML ecosystem, or how it can be a  game-changer in NAS research. It is limited in its range of NAS algorithms and search spaces. I recommend rejection.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer2
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the detailed feedback and the points raised. We now answer the reviewer’s questions.

1. **The motivation for doing this is sound, as reproducibility is a key problem in NAS [...]. However, actual implementation seems limited.**: Thank you for sharing our motivation. We agree that the implementation of NASLib is far from being finished, however when designing it we have had in mind several scenarios that might be of general interest to NAS researchers. To this end, we believe that the search space objects, NAS optimizers and evaluators are quite generic which allow implementing a wide range of spaces, algorithms and searching/training pipelines.

2. **it doesn’t appear to me that this codebase allows NAS researchers to do anything new.**: We apologize for the confusion. With NASLib NAS researchers can implement their proposed method in a simple yet very flexible fashion and conduct apples-to-apples comparisons to other baselines with just a few lines of code. This is regardless whether they contribute an optimizer, a new search space or even a different evaluation pipeline. This fosters reproducibility and fair comparisons. A concrete example, that we also provide now in the updated paper (see Table 2), is the fact that one can run weight-sharing NAS methods such as DARTS on the hierarchical search space from [1]. Note that with NASLib this requires only changing the search space object; the interface to the NAS optimizer remains the same as for other search spaces. To the best of our knowledge this has not been tackled before. 

3. **It is quite sparse in terms of the actual spaces and optimisers defined. There is an emphasis on one-shot methods and no code for REINFORCE. [...]. The list of improvements planned in the paper emphasises that this is not finished work.**: We agree with the reviewer. We are currently adding more optimizers (including discrete ones) and search spaces to the library. We are fully aware that NASLib is not yet mature and comprehensive, but we are confident that with time and the joint efforts of the community it will become a standard library for NAS research.

4. **Why should I use this library over those libraries [archai, aw-nas]? What are the functional differences, limitations etc.**: Thank you for raising this point. We will add a more comprehensive comparison to the next version of the paper.

5. **The DARTS performance in Table 1 is very different. Is there an obvious reason for this?**: Thank you for raising this point. We have now fixed several issues that had impeded exactly reproducing results in the original papers of the provided algorithms in NASLib. It seems that there are still some open issues and we are currently working on resolving them.

6. **There are no research contributions, the technical contributions seem limited. I don’t see what this library provides that doesn’t already exist in the ML ecosystem, or how it can be a game-changer in NAS research. It is limited in its range of NAS algorithms and search spaces.**: Thank you for your points. We believe that the ability of implementing methods on the same code base and having optimizers disentangled from specific search spaces could be a game changer in NAS research. As an example - to the best of our knowledge - we were the first to run one-shot optimizers on the hierarchical search space from [1] reducing the search cost by a factor of 1000.

-- References --

[1] Liu et al. Hierarchical Representations for Efficient Architecture Search. In ICLR 2017

content.title: Need to provide better proof to support claims
content.review:
##########################################################################

Summary:
The paper presents a framework for development and creation of Neural Architecture Search (NAS) algorithms.
NASLib structure is broken down into 3 blocks: search space, optimizer and trainer/evaluator.
The authors demonstrated some use-case: DARTs, NAS-bench201 and one-shot model on hierarchical search space.

##########################################################################

Reasons for score: 
The authors claim easy-to-use modular library and minimal prototyping time. However there is no measure of how easy or how well accepted this tool is in the dev community.

NASLib is built upon other libraries: pytorch and NetworkX. Some features claimed are native pytorch or other library features: checkpointing, data loading, logging. It is hard to discern what is a differential between this library from all others NAS libraries.
The paper does not provide proof or examples that NASLib is supperior than others more mature and well accepted frameworks: NNI, AutoGluon, Auto-Keras. 

##########################################################################: 
Pros: 
- flexibility to combine some NAS methods

##########################################################################
Cons:
- no clear evidence that is better than others
- no metric of ease of use
- well acceptance in dev community
- hard to distiguish the features from other built in libraries 

##########################################################################

Questions during rebuttal period: 
Please address and clarify the cons above

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer3
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer very much for the detailed review. We now answer the reviewer’s questions.

1. **no clear evidence that is better than others**: We apologize for the confusion. Our goal with creating NASLib was *not* to create an AutoML library like AutoGluon or Auto-Keras. We intend the library to be used for NAS researchers to provide an easy-to-use interface for creating both new search spaces and optimizers for a fast apples-to-apples comparison with all relevant baselines. We will try to make this point clearer in the paper.

2. **no metric of ease of use**: Thanks for raising this point! We agree with the reviewer that it might not be clear from the paper to assess usability. We tried to show with code snippets 1, 3, and 4 how simple it is to run NASLib, add a new search space and a new optimizer. However we are currently not aware of any metric regarding ease of use. We would appreciate it if the reviewer would point us to one. We would be very happy to include it in the paper.

3. **well acceptance in the dev community**: We agree that NASLib is not widely used yet. This is due to the fact that it was open-sourced just recently. We hope that, as we add more and more features, the community will accept it as a useful tool.

4. **hard to distinguish the features from other built in libraries (checkpointing, data loading, logging)**: Thank you for raising this point and we apologize for the confusion. The point we were trying to make by mentioning these features is that they are already included in NASLib and users do not have to worry about these little yet often time consuming parts of their experiments.

display_title: The results are good but novelty is not enough

content.title: The results are good but novelty is not enough
content.review:
This paper builds a library NASLib towards NAS which integrates the core parts, including search spaces, optimizers and trainers/evaluators, into a modularized framework. NASLib may help researchers to easily develop individual NAS components.

Strengths
1. The built library can facilitate implementation or developing NAS methods. This stream of works will be benefit for the community, which eliminate the burden of human engineers.
2. NAS methods implemented in NASLib achieve comparable results with that released in the original related papers. The code is attached for better reproduction.

Weaknesses
1. My main concern lies in how broad impact this paper can bring. The built library only involves the DAG (directed acyclic graph) cell-based search spaces. However, this type of search spaces normally bears high hardware latency, due to the complicated topology structures. Recently, block-based search spaces, e.g. MobileNet, ShuffleNet, have achieved great success in the NAS field. Though the blocks of theses search spaces may also be represented as a particular case of a DAG, how well the library can be generalized to more types of search spaces should be clarified. It is suggested to integrate the block-based search space and compare with some important works, e.g. ProxylessNAS[1], FBNet[2]. Moreover, multi-objective optimization is commonly performed in nowadays NAS methods but not mentioned in this paper. It seems many advanced technologies of NAS are missing in the library, which makes me concern about the impact of this work.
2. This is a promising engineering project. Does this paper carry any academic novelty? This should be explained.
3. In many cases, the small scale dataset is not enough to evaluate the method due to the large variance of the final results. The large scale dataset, e.g. ImageNet, is required to be included. Related experimental results need to be reported.
4. The codes of DARTS and GDAS are all released and widely used. Though this works integrates more modularized parts, is there any other advantage over the original projects?

[1] Cai H, Zhu L, Han S. Proxylessnas: Direct neural architecture search on target task and hardware[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:1812.00332, 2018.
[2] Wu B, Dai X, Zhang P, et al. Fbnet: Hardware-aware efficient convnet design via differentiable neural architecture search[C]//Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2019: 10734-10742.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer1
content.comment:
Thank you very much for your detailed review. In the following we answer the reviewer’s questions:

1. **”My main concern lies in how broad impact this paper can bring. The built library only involves the DAG (directed acyclic graph) cell-based search spaces. However, this type of search spaces normally bears high hardware latency, due to the complicated topology structures. Recently, block-based search spaces, e.g. MobileNet, ShuffleNet, have achieved great success in the NAS field. [...]”**: Thank you for raising this point! We are aware that these particular search spaces and multi-objective optimization are of particular importance in the current NAS research. We are currently working on integrating these. As you assumed, the flexible and generic search space representation in NASLib can definitely support such spaces since they can be represented as a DAG.

2. **”This is a promising engineering project. Does this paper carry any academic novelty? This should be explained.”**: Thank you for the encouraging words! We believe that NASLib can lead to a vast variety of combinations of different elements coming from different methods since each of them is or will be implemented on the same codebase. Therefore mixing and matching these should be easy for the researchers. As an example, we already run one-shot NAS optimizers in the hierarchical search space from [1]. In the original paper evolution was used to optimize the architecture and to the best of our knowledge this space has not been tackled before in the context of one-shot NAS. Moreover, our recent results (now in the experiments section in the updated paper) seem better or competitive to the original evolutionary method and are 1000x faster (of course this is due to the weight-sharing).

3. **”The large scale dataset, e.g. ImageNet, is required to be included. Related experimental results need to be reported.”**: We agree with the reviewer on this point. We will update the paper in future versions with these experiments.

4. **”The codes of DARTS and GDAS are all released and widely used. Though this work integrates more modularized parts, is there any other advantage over the original projects?”**: True, the codebases for DARTS and GDAS are already released, however, they do not allow for a quick modularization of novel solutions. We reengineered the solutions in a modular fashion to enable quick exploration of novel ideas that combine new search spaces with new optimizers and new evaluation pipelines. 

-- References --

[1] Liu et al. Hierarchical Representations for Efficient Architecture Search. In ICLR 2017

content.title: Official Blind review #4
content.review:
Summary:
This paper proposes and introduces a Neural architecture search library built on pytorch which provides high level abstractions for designing search spaces, common interfaces to datasets and benchmarks such as Nasbench-201 and Nasbench-301, and extensible implementations of some Neural Architecture Search(NAS) methods. The library is designed to help facilitate scientific research and reproducibility for NAS. The library aims to streamline into one framework implementations for both discrete and weight-sharing based algorithms in a way that the algorithms themselves are agnostic to the search spaces. They demonstrate their framework by reproducing results for several algorithms such as DARTS and GDAS. They show how DARTS can easily be applied even to hierarchical search spacings using their modular formulation.

Pros:
	1. Provides a modular framework for Neural Architecture Search which could encourage easy reproducibility and accelerate Neural Architecture Search research.
	2. Flexible and modular framework for defining search spaces.
	3. Provides a great interface to evaluate on Nas-bench and benchmark datasets.
	4. 

Cons:
	1. Unclear support or documentation on multi-gpu and distributed training support limits the usability for larger scale experiments. Better documentation and support and results for larger scale experiments would greatly improve the submission.
	2. It's somewhat unclear how close the implementations reproduce original results. For example, the GDAS results on CIFAR 10 seem to achieve much worse performance than was reported at twice the parameter cost while using 10x the search cost. Uncertainty could limit it's usage for strong baselines. Additional work on the search algorithms would be of great benefit to demonstrate the flexibility and extensibility of the framework.
	3. Would benefit from more documentation since the usage and api for things such as the trainer is somewhat unclear. 


Reasons for score: 
Overall, I weakly recommend rejecting this paper. Without a doubt I believe that a unified architecture search library is truly beneficial to the field and would help accelerate architecture search research. It would be of great benefit to be able to provide strong baseline comparisons without every author having to search and integrate algorithm implementations into their training pipeline. The framework most notably provides very helpful tools to access the nas-bench datasets and a flexible framework for defining search spaces. However, it's not entirely clear that this framework is entirely mature enough, especially related to it's documentation, algorithms, and training support, but could be invaluable with improvements. 

Questions:
How extensible is naslib for multi-gpu and distributed NAS?
One-shot NAS is discussed several times in relation to weight-sharing approaches, but it's somewhat unclear if results are shown after one training epoch or supernet training?
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer4
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their useful feedback and for appreciating our efforts towards a unified and flexible neural architecture search library! Below we provide answers to each the listed concerns:

1. **“Unclear support or documentation on multi-gpu and distributed training support limits the usability for larger scale experiments. Better documentation and support and results for larger scale experiments would greatly improve the submission.”**: We are currently working on providing a multi-gpu training for both single models using DistributedDataParallel and black-box NAS optimizers such as Random Search to parallelize the training of single networks across cluster nodes.

2. **”It's somewhat unclear how close the implementations reproduce original results. For example, the GDAS results on CIFAR 10 seem to achieve much worse performance than was reported at twice the parameter cost while using 10x the search cost. Uncertainty could limit it's usage for strong baselines. Additional work on the search algorithms would be of great benefit to demonstrate the flexibility and extensibility of the framework.”**: We fully agree with the reviewer on this point. We have now fixed several issues that had impeded reproducing speed results in the original papers of the provided algorithms in NASLib. Furthermore, we are working on adding more and more optimizers to the library, using the same interface to the search spaces as the ones already implemented.

3. **”Would benefit from more documentation since the usage and api for things such as the trainer is somewhat unclear.”**: Thank you! We will provide detailed documentation shortly, together with the public release of the library.

4. **”Without a doubt I believe that a unified architecture search library is truly beneficial to the field and would help accelerate architecture search research. [...] However, it's not entirely clear that this framework is entirely mature enough, especially related to it's documentation, algorithms, and training support, but could be invaluable with improvements.”**: Thank you for your kind words! We agree and are fully aware that NASLib is at its first baby steps right now, but we are quite confident that with time and the joint efforts of the community it will become a standard library for NAS research.

5. **”How extensible is naslib for multi-gpu and distributed NAS?”**: As we mentioned above, we are working on both of these at the moment and in release 1.0 NASLib will support both these functionalities. 
6. **”One-shot NAS is discussed several times in relation to weight-sharing approaches, but it's somewhat unclear if results are shown after one training epoch or supernet training?”**: We apologize for the confusion. As the reviewer assumed, the results in plots such as the ones in Fig. 2 and Fig. 4 show the test performance of the architectures retrained from scratch (actually in this case queried from the benchmarks) at each one-shot training epoch.

content.title: Decision to withdraw
content.comment:
We would like to thank all reviewers for their valuable feedback. We are aware that the library is not fully mature, however our hope was that the NAS research community would welcome a paper with a recent library which offers new design principles on re-engineering NAS methods in a fully modular fashion.  In that way, the publication would have served to spread the word in  the community to participate and contribute to improving the library further, since a mature library can only be achieved as a joint contribution of a community, rather than by the isolated efforts of one research team. The paper, we hoped, would motivate the community to foster efforts into a NAS library for researchers.

We share the positive criticism that the library would benefit from more experiments, algorithms and search spaces added. We therefore withdraw our submission in order to complete the requested parts and submit an improved version in the future.

Nevertheless we still encourage everyone to use NASLib (https://github.com/automl/NASLib) for experiments and welcome all contributions by the community!
